title: NMR Principles: Spin, Shift, Coupling, Relaxation
description: Larmor precession, chemical shift origins, J-coupling, and the T1/T2 timescales that govern every NMR experiment

concepts.title: Spin, Larmor Frequency, and the Boltzmann Population
concepts.contentHtml:
NMR works because nuclei with non-zero spin (1H, 13C, 15N, 19F, 31P) behave as tiny magnets. In an external field B0, the spin states split by energy ΔE = γℏB0, where γ is the nuclear gyromagnetic ratio. The resulting precession frequency, the Larmor frequency, is ν0 = γB0/2π.

For 1H on a Bruker Avance Neo 600 (B0 = 14.1 T), γ = 2.675×108 rad·s−1·T−1 gives ν0 ≈ 600 MHz. 13C at the same field precesses near 150 MHz because γ(13C) is roughly a quarter of γ(1H).

NMR is a low-sensitivity technique because the Boltzmann population difference is minuscule: at 600 MHz and 298 K, the upper-state excess is only ~5×10−5. That is why you average for hours, why 13C at 1.1 % natural abundance is so much harder than 1H, and why cryoprobes (cooled preamplifier coils) and dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) deliver such dramatic gains.

concepts.title: Chemical Shift and Scalar (J) Coupling
concepts.contentHtml:
Electrons around a nucleus partially shield it from B0, so the actual local field is Blocal = B0(1 − σ). The dimensionless chemical shift δ in ppm is referenced (for 1H and 13C) to TMS at 0 ppm: δ = (νsample − νref)/νref × 106.

Familiar 1H benchmarks: alkyl CH3 0.9 ppm; CH2 next to oxygen 3.5–4.5 ppm; vinyl 5–6 ppm; aromatic 6.5–8.5 ppm; aldehyde 9.5–10 ppm; carboxylic acid 10–13 ppm. 13C: aliphatic 0–50 ppm, sp3-CO 50–90 ppm, sp2 100–150 ppm, carbonyl 160–220 ppm.

Scalar (J) coupling reports through-bond electron-mediated interaction between nuclei, splitting peaks into multiplets. For an ethyl group, the CH3 appears as a triplet from the two neighboring protons (n+1 rule, J ≈ 7 Hz) and the CH2 as a quartet. 3JHH obeys the Karplus relation, J(θ) = A cos2θ + B cosθ + C, allowing dihedral angles to be read straight off a spectrum.

concepts.title: T1, T2, and the Nuclear Overhauser Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
After an RF pulse tilts magnetization, two distinct relaxation processes return it to equilibrium. T1 (spin–lattice) is energy exchange with the environment, restoring Mz. T2 (spin–spin) is loss of phase coherence in the xy-plane and sets the natural linewidth: Δν1/2 = 1/(πT2). Small molecules in low-viscosity solvent have T1 ≈ T2 ≈ a few seconds; proteins in water tumble slowly so T2 collapses to milliseconds, broadening lines dramatically.

Practical consequence: the recycle delay between scans should be ~5·T1 for full quantitative recovery. 13C of a quaternary carbon can have T1 > 30 s — measure it before quantifying.

The Nuclear Overhauser Effect (NOE) is a through-space (not through-bond) cross-relaxation that transfers polarization between dipolar-coupled nuclei within ~5 Å. NOE intensities scale as r−6, making 2D NOESY spectra into a distance ruler used to determine solution structures of proteins, oligonucleotides, and complex natural products.

title: 1D NMR in Practice: 1H, 13C, and DEPT
description: Multiplicity, integration, common shifts, and the DEPT edited-13C trick

concepts.title: Reading a 1H Spectrum: Shift, Integration, Multiplicity
concepts.contentHtml:
A 1H spectrum encodes three pieces of information per peak. Chemical shift identifies the chemical environment. Integration (the area under the peak) gives the number of equivalent protons. Multiplicity reports the number of vicinal coupled protons via the n+1 rule.

Consider ethyl acetate, CH3COOCH2CH3, in CDCl3. The acetyl CH3 sits at 2.05 ppm as a 3H singlet (no neighbors). The OCH2 appears at 4.12 ppm as a 2H quartet (J ≈ 7.1 Hz, coupled to three CH3 protons). The CH3 of the ethoxy group sits at 1.26 ppm as a 3H triplet, the same J. Three signals; integration ratio 3:2:3 confirms the formula.

Solvent peaks anchor the spectrum: CDCl3 residual CHCl3 at 7.26 ppm, DMSO-d6 at 2.50 ppm, D2O HOD at 4.79 ppm. Exchangeable protons (OH, NH) often disappear or shift unpredictably and can be confirmed by a D2O shake (the peak vanishes when exchangeable H is replaced by D).

concepts.title: 13C and Heteronuclear Decoupling
concepts.contentHtml:
13C NMR is acquired with broadband 1H decoupling, which collapses every C–H multiplet into a singlet and harvests an NOE enhancement (up to 3×). The trade: integration is no longer quantitative because NOE depends on local proton environment. For quantitative 13C, use inverse-gated decoupling and a long recycle delay (5·T1, often 30–60 s).

Anchoring shifts: TMS 0.0 ppm; CDCl3 solvent triplet 77.16 ppm; aromatic carbons 110–150 ppm; carbonyl carbons 165–185 ppm for esters/amides, 205–220 ppm for ketones, 190–205 ppm for aldehydes, 170–180 ppm for carboxylic acids.

On a typical 600 MHz Bruker spectrometer, a 10 mg sample of a small molecule in 0.6 mL CDCl3 needs only minutes for a clean 1H spectrum but often hours for a clean 13C — the gyromagnetic ratio ratio (γH/γC)3 ≈ 64 plus 1.1 % natural abundance puts 13C sensitivity ~5700× below 1H per nucleus.

concepts.title: DEPT and Multiplicity Editing
concepts.contentHtml:
DEPT (Distortionless Enhancement by Polarization Transfer) uses a tunable proton pulse angle θ to edit a 13C spectrum by C–H multiplicity. With θ = 90°, only CH carbons appear. With θ = 135° (the most common), CH and CH3 point up while CH2 points down; quaternary C is invisible. With θ = 45°, all protonated carbons point up, quaternary still invisible.

Comparing a normal 13C and a DEPT-135 of the same sample reveals every quaternary carbon as a peak missing from DEPT — invaluable in natural product structure elucidation, where quaternary centers are often the structural anchors.

DEPT is a polarization transfer experiment: it borrows magnetization from 1H to 13C through one-bond 1JCH coupling (~125–250 Hz), so signal scales by γH/γC ≈ 4 compared to direct excitation. Modern multiplicity-edited HSQC essentially achieves DEPT editing along with the 2D HSQC correlation in the same experiment, but DEPT remains useful when 1D resolution is enough.

title: 2D NMR: COSY, HSQC, HMBC, NOESY
description: Through-bond and through-space correlations and the structure-elucidation workflow

concepts.title: The 2D NMR Pulse Sequence Recipe
concepts.contentHtml:
Every 2D NMR experiment shares the same skeleton: preparation – evolution (t1) – mixing – detection (t2). Magnetization is prepared (often a 90° pulse), evolves under chemical shift and coupling for incremented time t1, gets mixed (the step that defines the experiment — coupling, polarization transfer, NOE), then is detected during t2. A 2D Fourier transform over both time domains produces a frequency-frequency map.

Diagonal peaks (F1 = F2) connect a nucleus to itself; cross peaks reveal correlations. The cross-peak meaning depends on the mixing block: J-coupling (COSY, TOCSY), one-bond 1H–13C (HSQC), long-range 1H–13C (HMBC), through-space dipolar (NOESY, ROESY).

Sensitivity scales with √(number of t1 increments); a typical heteronuclear 2D on a Bruker 600 MHz Avance with cryoprobe takes 30 min to a few hours for a 5 mg sample, vs. overnight on a room-temperature probe. Non-uniform sampling (NUS) can shave acquisition time by 4–8× by sampling only a fraction of t1 points and reconstructing the spectrum with iterative algorithms.

concepts.title: COSY, TOCSY, HSQC, HMBC
concepts.contentHtml:
COSY (Correlation Spectroscopy) is the simplest 2D experiment: 1H–1H cross peaks identify scalar (J) coupling partners, almost always 2- or 3-bond. Trace cross peaks across the spectrum to walk along a spin system.

TOCSY (Total Correlation Spectroscopy) uses an isotropic mixing block (DIPSI or MLEV) to spread magnetization across an entire J-coupled spin system. One row of a TOCSY spectrum lights up every proton in the same coupling network — invaluable for assigning peptide spin systems or sugar rings in oligosaccharides.

HSQC and HMBC are heteronuclear. HSQC correlates a proton with its directly bonded heteronucleus via 1JCH (~145 Hz default). HMBC correlates 1H with 2- and 3-bond distant carbons via nJCH (~5–10 Hz). HMBC is the workhorse for connecting fragments across quaternary carbons and heteroatoms — e.g., locating an ester linkage by seeing the OCH2 proton correlate to the carbonyl carbon three bonds away. Modern variants (CIGAR-HMBC, ADEQUATE) push selectivity even further.

concepts.title: NOESY and the Structure-Elucidation Workflow
concepts.contentHtml:
NOESY cross peaks come from through-space dipolar coupling and decay as r−6; cross peak intensity → distance, with practical reach of about 5 Å. NOESY is how solution structures of small proteins, RNA, and stereochemically rich natural products are determined: hundreds of NOE distance restraints feed a simulated annealing protocol (Xplor-NIH, CYANA) to compute a 3D structure.

For molecules with τc ≈ 1/ω0 (typically MW 1000–2000 in standard solvents), the NOE crosses zero. ROESY (rotating-frame NOE) escapes the zero-crossing and gives positive cross peaks at any size.

The classical structure elucidation workflow: (1) 1D 1H + 13C/DEPT to count C and H environments; (2) COSY/TOCSY to map proton spin systems; (3) HSQC to attach each proton to its carbon; (4) HMBC to splice spin systems through quaternary centers and heteroatoms; (5) NOESY to fix relative stereochemistry and conformation. Modern computer-assisted tools (LSD, SENECA, MNova) automate fragment assembly.

title: Solid-State NMR: MAS and Cross-Polarization
description: Spinning the sample at the magic angle to recover liquid-like resolution from rocks, polymers, and proteins

concepts.title: Why Solids Are Hard: Anisotropic Interactions
concepts.contentHtml:
In solution, fast molecular tumbling averages anisotropic interactions to zero, leaving sharp lines. In a powder or a protein crystal, three large interactions remain orientation-dependent. Chemical shift anisotropy (CSA) can span 200 ppm for carbonyls. Dipolar coupling between 1H and 13C reaches ~25 kHz; between two protons, ~120 kHz. Quadrupolar coupling for spin > 1/2 nuclei (2H, 14N, 17O) reaches MHz. The result without intervention: featureless 100 kHz-wide lumps where you wanted 1 Hz lines.

The trick is magic angle spinning (MAS): physically spin the rotor at angle θm = arccos(1/√3) ≈ 54.74° to B0. The dipolar Hamiltonian and CSA both contain the geometric factor (3cos²θ − 1), which vanishes at this angle. Spin fast enough (faster than the interaction strength) and the powder pattern collapses to isotropic-like lines plus spinning sidebands at multiples of the MAS rate.

Modern probes spin 1.3 mm rotors at 60–110 kHz; emerging 0.7 mm rotors push beyond 150 kHz, fast enough to nearly remove the strongest 1H–1H dipolar couplings and enable proton-detected protein ssNMR.

concepts.title: Cross-Polarization and DNP
concepts.contentHtml:
Cross-polarization (CP) transfers magnetization from abundant 1H to dilute, slowly-relaxing nuclei (13C, 15N) via simultaneous spin-lock pulses on both channels. The Hartmann–Hahn condition γHB1H = γXB1X matches the rotating-frame energy gap and lets dipolar coupling shuttle polarization across. Result: signal enhancement up to γH/γX (~4 for 13C) and a much shorter recycle delay set by the (faster) 1H T1.

For 13C and 15N work on Bruker and JEOL solid-state probes, CPMAS (cross-polarization with MAS) is the default: ramped CP, contact times 0.5–2 ms, MAS 10–14 kHz, high-power TPPM or SPINAL64 1H decoupling during acquisition.

Dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) goes further: dope the sample with a stable biradical (TOTAPOL, AMUPol), cool to ~100 K, irradiate the electron EPR transition with a gyrotron-generated microwave (~263 GHz at 9.4 T), and electron polarization (γe/γH ≈ 660) transfers to nearby protons. Routine signal enhancements of 50–200× on commercial Bruker DNP-NMR systems make experiments feasible that would otherwise require months of averaging.

concepts.title: Applications: Catalysts, Membranes, Batteries
concepts.contentHtml:
Solid-state NMR sees what diffraction misses: amorphous regions, disordered surfaces, and dynamics on µs–ms timescales. Heterogeneous catalysts: 27Al MAS distinguishes 4-, 5-, and 6-coordinate Al in zeolites by chemical shift (60, 30, 0 ppm respectively); 29Si MAS resolves Q4, Q3, Q2 silicate environments differing by 10 ppm each.

Membrane proteins: amyloid fibrils, GPCRs in lipid bilayers, and bacterial cell walls have all been solved by ssNMR using 13C, 15N labeling and dipolar recoupling sequences (PDSD, DARR, RFDR) that reintroduce the dipolar coupling that MAS removed, encoding distances. Influenza M2 channel and amyloid-β fibril structures are landmark ssNMR results on systems that crystallography struggles with.

Batteries: 7Li and 23Na MAS NMR follows lithium environments inside operating Li-ion electrodes, identifies plated Li metal vs intercalated Li, and quantifies SEI components in real time. 17O DNP on lithium-ion cathodes (LiCoO2, LiFePO4) reveals oxygen redox chemistry that controls cycling stability.

title: IR, Raman, and Surface-Enhanced Raman
description: Vibrational fingerprints, mutual-exclusion rules, and the SERS plasmonic enhancement

concepts.title: Selection Rules and Group Frequencies
concepts.contentHtml:
Vibrational spectroscopy probes molecular vibrations whose energies sit in the IR (mid-IR 400–4000 cm−1). Each normal mode has frequency ν̃ = (1/2πc)√(k/μ), where k is the bond force constant and μ is the reduced mass — heavier atoms or weaker bonds give lower frequencies.

The IR selection rule requires a mode to change the dipole moment to be active. The Raman selection rule requires a change in polarizability. For centrosymmetric molecules (CO2, benzene), these are mutually exclusive: gerade modes are Raman-only, ungerade modes are IR-only.

Group frequencies anchor interpretation. O–H stretch 3200–3550 cm−1 (broad, H-bonded). N–H stretch 3300–3500 cm−1. C–H stretch 2850–3100 cm−1. C≡N 2200–2260 cm−1. C=O stretch 1670–1820 cm−1 (acid 1700–1725, ketone 1705–1725, amide I 1640–1690, ester 1735–1750). Below 1500 cm−1 sits the fingerprint region, dense and largely diagnostic by overall pattern matching against libraries (Sigma-Aldrich, NIST).

concepts.title: FTIR and Raman Instrumentation
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern IR spectrometers (Thermo Nicolet iS50, Bruker Vertex 70, PerkinElmer Spectrum 3) are Fourier-transform IR (FTIR): a Michelson interferometer with a moving mirror produces an interferogram, and a Fourier transform yields the spectrum. FTIR's multiplex (Fellgett) advantage measures all wavelengths at once, and the throughput (Jacquinot) advantage dispenses with slits, giving SNR orders of magnitude better than dispersive IR.

Attenuated Total Reflection (ATR) accessories with diamond or ZnSe crystals enable solid/liquid sampling without preparation: an evanescent wave penetrates ~1 µm into the sample. ATR-FTIR is the workhorse of pharma QC and forensics today.

Raman spectrometers excite with a monochromatic laser (532 nm green, 785 nm NIR, or 1064 nm to suppress fluorescence) and detect inelastically scattered light shifted by molecular vibrations. Raman cross sections are tiny (~10−30 cm2), roughly 1013–1014 times smaller than fluorescence cross sections — until SERS changes the game.

concepts.title: Surface-Enhanced Raman (SERS)
concepts.contentHtml:
Adsorb a molecule onto a roughened metal surface (Au, Ag) and Raman scattering can intensify by 106–1011×. The dominant mechanism is electromagnetic enhancement: the laser excites localized surface plasmon resonances on metal nanostructures, generating intense near-fields that scale signal as |Elocal|4. A secondary chemical enhancement contributes ~10–100× via charge transfer between adsorbate and metal.

At hot spots — the gap between two nanoparticles or a sharp tip-to-surface junction — the field reaches enhancements of 1010–1012, enough for single-molecule SERS first reported by Nie and Kneipp in 1997. Nanostructured commercial substrates (Hamamatsu, Ocean Insight, Renishaw) deliver reproducible enhancement of 106–108, sufficient for trace detection of pesticides, explosives, drugs, and neurotransmitters at picomolar concentration.

Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS) combines AFM/STM with a sharpened plasmonic tip, achieving spatial resolution ~10 nm and even sub-nm at low temperature — vibrational spectra of individual molecules with chemical-bond imaging.

title: Mass Spectrometry: Ionization, Analyzers, Fragmentation
description: From EI and ESI to Orbitrap and FT-ICR, plus exact mass and isotope pattern interpretation

concepts.title: Ionization Methods: EI, ESI, MALDI
concepts.contentHtml:
Mass spectrometry needs gas-phase ions; how you make them shapes the spectrum. Electron ionization (EI, 70 eV) bombards vaporized neutrals with energetic electrons, producing radical cations M+• and extensive fragmentation. EI is reproducible enough that NIST spectral libraries (>350,000 entries) make GC-EI-MS the gold standard for small-molecule identification.

Electrospray ionization (ESI), the 2002 Nobel-winning Fenn technique, sprays liquid through a charged capillary at atmospheric pressure, producing multiply-charged [M+nH]n+ ions for proteins or [M+H]+, [M+Na]+, [M−H]− for small molecules. ESI is gentle and ideal for LC-MS coupling — the hyphenated technique behind virtually all modern proteomics, metabolomics, and pharma DMPK.

MALDI (Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization) co-crystallizes analyte with a UV-absorbing matrix (CHCA, sinapinic acid, DHB) on a metal target; a 337 nm N2 laser pulse generates predominantly singly-charged [M+H]+. Excellent for proteins, polymers, and now MALDI imaging: rastering the laser across a tissue section produces molecular images of metabolites, lipids, and drugs at 5–20 µm resolution.
mathExpressions: n = \frac{m_2 - 1.00728}{m_1 - m_2} \quad \text{(charge from two adjacent peaks)}

concepts.title: Mass Analyzers: TOF, Orbitrap, FT-ICR
concepts.contentHtml:
Resolving power R = m/Δm distinguishes ions of similar mass. Quadrupole (R ~1000) is cheap, fast, robust — the workhorse of routine LC-MS. Time-of-flight (TOF) measures flight time across a field-free drift tube: lighter ions arrive first, with t = L√(m/2zU). Modern reflectron-TOFs (Bruker timsTOF, Waters Synapt, AB Sciex TripleTOF) deliver R ~50,000 with mass accuracy <2 ppm.

The Orbitrap (Makarov, 2000; commercialized by Thermo Fisher as Exactive, Q Exactive, Orbitrap Eclipse, Orbitrap Astral) traps ions in a logarithmic radial potential around a spindle electrode; ions oscillate axially with frequency ω = √(k/m). An image-current detector + Fourier transform yields R up to 1,000,000 and sub-ppm mass accuracy. The Orbitrap reshaped proteomics by combining Q-MS2 selectivity with high-resolution accurate-mass detection.

FT-ICR traps ions in a Penning cell, exciting cyclotron motion at ωc = qB/m; at 21 T (Bruker solariX XR, the ultra-high-field FT-ICR at NHMFL), R exceeds 10,000,000 and mass accuracy reaches sub-ppb. Indispensable for crude oil characterization (petroleomics) where 30,000 distinct molecular formulas may coexist.

concepts.title: Exact Mass and Isotope Patterns
concepts.contentHtml:
At sub-ppm mass accuracy, the exact mass of an ion uniquely (often) determines its molecular formula. 12C = 12.000000 by definition; 1H = 1.007825; 14N = 14.003074; 16O = 15.994915; 32S = 31.972071. Caffeine C8H10N4O2 has nominal mass 194 but monoisotopic mass 194.080376 — distinguishable from C10H14N2O2 (194.105528) at any R > 8000.

The nitrogen rule: an organic molecule with an odd nominal mass contains an odd number of nitrogens (only N has odd valence and even nominal mass).

Isotope patterns tag elements at a glance. Cl gives a 3:1 [M]:[M+2] doublet (35Cl/37Cl, 76:24). Br gives 1:1 [M]:[M+2]. S gives a small [M+2] (~4 % per S from 34S). For a molecule with n carbons, the [M+1] peak is ~1.1n % of M from 13C natural abundance — counting carbons by isotope pattern is a one-line check on a candidate formula.

title: Tandem MS and Proteomics
description: MS/MS fragmentation, b/y peptide ions, DDA vs DIA, and label-free quantification

concepts.title: Tandem MS: CID, HCD, ETD, UVPD
concepts.contentHtml:
Tandem MS (MS/MS) selects a precursor ion in MS1, fragments it, and analyzes the products in MS2. The selectivity transforms MS from a molecular weight tool into a sequencing tool.

Collision-Induced Dissociation (CID), performed in a quadrupole or linear ion trap, uses inert gas (Ar, N2, He) collisions to deposit vibrational energy that breaks the weakest bonds. Higher-energy Collisional Dissociation (HCD) on Orbitrap-class instruments uses a separate collision cell; energies are higher and immonium ions appear, giving more comprehensive peptide spectra.

Electron Transfer Dissociation (ETD) transfers an electron from a radical anion (typically fluoranthene−•) to a multiply-charged peptide, cleaving N–Cα bonds and producing c/z• ions while preserving labile post-translational modifications like phosphorylation, glycosylation, and sulfation. UVPD (Ultraviolet Photodissociation) with 193 nm excimer lasers fragments more uniformly across the backbone and is especially powerful for top-down proteomics on intact proteins. Modern Orbitrap Tribrid instruments offer all four modes selectable per scan.

concepts.title: Peptide Fragmentation: b and y Ions
concepts.contentHtml:
Roepstorff–Biemann nomenclature labels peptide backbone fragments by which side keeps the charge: a, b, c from the N-terminus; x, y, z from the C-terminus. CID/HCD predominantly produce b ions (acylium-like, charge on N-side after CO–NH cleavage) and y ions (charge on C-side, +1 H2O). ETD produces c and z• ions from N–Cα cleavage.

Mass differences between consecutive b (or y) ions equal residue masses, letting the peptide sequence be read off the spectrum: G = 57.02, A = 71.04, S = 87.03, P = 97.05, V = 99.07, T = 101.05, C = 103.01, L/I = 113.08 (isomers with identical mass, so MS1 alone cannot tell them apart), N = 114.04, D = 115.03, Q = 128.06, K = 128.09 (close to Q!), E = 129.04, M = 131.04, H = 137.06, F = 147.07, R = 156.10, Y = 163.06, W = 186.08.

Database search engines (SEQUEST, Mascot, MaxQuant Andromeda, MSFragger, Comet) match observed MS2 spectra against in-silico digests of FASTA proteome databases, scoring with statistical models and applying target-decoy FDR control (typically 1 %).

concepts.title: DDA vs DIA and Label-Free Quantification
concepts.contentHtml:
Data-Dependent Acquisition (DDA) is the classical shotgun proteomics workflow: an MS1 survey scan picks the top N (usually 10–20) most intense precursors, isolates each in turn (~1.6 m/z window), fragments them, and collects MS2. Coverage depends on chromatographic peak picking and is stochastic — abundant peptides crowd out weak ones.

Data-Independent Acquisition (DIA / SWATH), pioneered on AB Sciex TripleTOF and now standard on Orbitrap Exploris and Astral, fragments everything in successive m/z windows (typically 4–25 m/z wide), producing chimeric MS2 spectra that are deconvolved with spectral libraries (Spectronaut, DIA-NN). Result: reproducible, comprehensive quantification across thousands of samples.

For label-free quantification, MaxQuant's MaxLFQ algorithm derives protein abundances from peptide MS1 intensities. For multiplexed quantification, TMT (tandem mass tags) attaches isobaric labels to up to 18 samples; reporter ions appear in MS2 (or MS3 SPS for accuracy) at low m/z (126–135). A modern Orbitrap Astral analyzes ~10,000 proteins per single-shot 30 min DIA run on a 5 µg HeLa digest.
mathExpressions: \text{DDA: select top } N \text{ precursors per MS}^1 \text{ cycle}

title: EPR/ESR and X-ray Spectroscopies
description: Electron spin spectroscopy and the X-ray techniques (XPS, XANES, EXAFS) that probe oxidation state and local geometry

concepts.title: EPR: g-Values, Hyperfine, and Spin Trapping
concepts.contentHtml:
EPR (electron paramagnetic resonance), also called ESR, is NMR's electron-spin cousin. The resonance condition hν = gμBB gives, for a free electron g = 2.0023, a frequency near 9.4 GHz at B ≈ 0.34 T (X-band, the standard Bruker EMXplus setup) — three orders of magnitude higher than typical NMR. The g-tensor is anisotropic and reports orbital character: ge for organic radicals, g ≈ 2.05 for Cu2+, large deviations for low-spin Fe3+.

The unpaired electron couples to nearby magnetic nuclei via hyperfine coupling A, splitting the EPR line into 2nI+1 components. A nitroxide radical (TEMPO, MTSL spin label) shows the iconic three-line spectrum from 14N (I = 1) with Aiso ≈ 14–17 G in solution.

Spin trapping uses diamagnetic traps (DMPO, PBN) to capture short-lived radicals like •OH and •O2− as stable nitroxide adducts; characteristic AN and AH values identify the original radical. Site-Directed Spin Labeling (SDSL) attaches MTSL to engineered cysteines on proteins, and CW EPR + DEER pulsed EPR (Bruker Elexsys E580) measure 2–8 nm distances between two labels — a structural ruler complementary to NMR and FRET.

concepts.title: XPS and Surface Composition
concepts.contentHtml:
X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS / ESCA) illuminates a surface with monochromatic Al Kα (1486.6 eV) or Mg Kα (1253.6 eV) X-rays and analyzes the kinetic energies of ejected core-level photoelectrons. The Einstein photoelectric equation gives BE = hν − KE − φ, where φ is the spectrometer work function. Each element has unique binding energies (NIST XPS database), and the inelastic mean free path of photoelectrons (~1–10 nm) makes XPS strictly surface-sensitive.

Beyond elemental ID, XPS resolves chemical states via 1–10 eV chemical shifts. C 1s sits at 284.8 eV for graphitic C, 286.5 for C–O, 288 for C=O, 289 for COOH/COOR. Si 2p sits at 99 eV for Si0, 103.4 for SiO2. Oxidation-state mapping of transition-metal catalysts and surface treatments uses these shifts directly.

Modern Thermo K-Alpha, Kratos Axis Supra, PHI VersaProbe instruments add imaging XPS (5–10 µm spot) and depth profiling via Ar+ or Ar cluster sputtering. Synchrotron-based HAXPES uses 5–10 keV X-rays for buried-interface depth (>20 nm) — invaluable for battery interfaces and gate stacks.

concepts.title: XAS: XANES and EXAFS
concepts.contentHtml:
X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy (XAS) tunes a synchrotron X-ray beam (e.g. APS, ESRF, Diamond, NSLS-II) across an element's absorption edge and measures the absorption coefficient. The spectrum splits into two regimes.

XANES (X-ray Absorption Near Edge Structure), within ±50 eV of the edge, encodes oxidation state (the edge shifts ~1–2 eV per oxidation unit) and coordination geometry (Pre-edge intensity in the Fe K-edge tells tetrahedral vs octahedral). XANES is used routinely to monitor operating fuel cells, Li-ion battery cycling, enzyme intermediates (cytochrome P450, photosystem II), and homogeneous catalysts in situ.

EXAFS (Extended X-ray Absorption Fine Structure), extending 50–1000 eV above the edge, contains oscillations χ(k) caused by interference between the outgoing photoelectron wave and waves backscattered from neighboring atoms. Fourier transform of k2χ(k) yields a pseudo-radial distribution: nearest-neighbor distances with ±0.02 Å precision and coordination numbers ±20 %. EXAFS works on amorphous and dilute samples where XRD fails — single-atom catalysts, metal sites in proteins, glasses.

title: Chiroptical and Nonlinear Vibrational Spectroscopy
description: VCD, ROA, SRS, and 2D-IR — pushing vibrational and chiral information further

concepts.title: ECD, VCD, and ROA: Vibrational Chiroptics
concepts.contentHtml:
Chiroptical methods directly probe molecular chirality. Electronic Circular Dichroism (ECD) measures differential absorption of left vs right circularly polarized UV light (Δε = εL − εR), reporting on chromophore environment — used routinely for protein secondary structure (α-helix shows minima at 208 and 222 nm; β-sheet a single 218 nm minimum). Modern instruments: JASCO J-1500, Applied Photophysics Chirascan.

Vibrational Circular Dichroism (VCD) extends CD to IR, measuring tiny (~10−4) absorbance differences across vibrational modes. Combined with DFT calculations (Gaussian, ADF) of theoretical VCD spectra for both enantiomers, VCD determines absolute configuration without crystallization — pharma uses it to confirm chirality of API and metabolites.

Raman Optical Activity (ROA) measures the difference in Raman scattering intensity for right vs left circularly polarized incident light. ROA is uniquely powerful for biomolecules in water (water transmits poorly in the IR); it has been used to fingerprint protein folds, virus capsids, and even intact bacteria. The signals are smaller still (~10−3–10−4 of the Raman intensity), demanding hours of integration on commercial BioTools ChiralRAMAN or research-grade instruments.

concepts.title: SRS, CARS, and Stimulated Raman Microscopy
concepts.contentHtml:
Spontaneous Raman is weak; nonlinear Raman is fast. Coherent Anti-Stokes Raman Scattering (CARS) uses two lasers — pump at ωp and Stokes at ωs — to coherently drive a vibration when ωp − ωs matches a Raman mode. A third pulse generates anti-Stokes signal at 2ωp − ωs, signal scales quadratically with concentration but rides a non-resonant background.

Stimulated Raman Scattering (SRS) microscopy, popularized by Xie and Min for cellular imaging, modulates one beam and detects amplitude transfer to the other. Signal is linear in concentration and free of non-resonant background — making it the gold-standard label-free vibrational microscopy. Commercial Leica TCS SP8 SRS, Olympus FV3000-multiphoton, and APE picoEmerald systems achieve diffraction-limited SRS imaging at video rate.

Applications include label-free imaging of myelin (CH2 stretch at 2845 cm−1), in vivo skin tumor identification by lipid:protein ratio, real-time histology during neurosurgery (Invenio Imaging SRH), and tracking small-molecule drugs by their unique fingerprint vibrations.

concepts.title: 2D-IR: Vibrational Couplings and Sub-ps Dynamics
concepts.contentHtml:
2D-IR spectroscopy is to IR what 2D NMR is to NMR — but six orders of magnitude faster. Three femtosecond mid-IR pulses drive vibrational coherences and probe their evolution: a 2D map (ωpump, ωprobe) appears, with diagonal peaks for each mode and off-diagonal cross peaks for vibrationally coupled modes.

Cross peaks reveal anharmonic coupling between, say, the amide-I C=O stretches of two residues in a peptide — protein structure on a 1 ps timescale. The waiting time Tw between pump and probe lets you watch spectral diffusion: how a frequency loses memory of its initial value as the local environment fluctuates, directly reporting on hydrogen-bond dynamics in water (~50 fs frequency-frequency correlation time) and protein–water interfaces.

Commercial 2D-IR systems (PhaseTech 2D Quick, Newport Spectra-Physics) build on Ti:sapphire-pumped OPAs producing 50–100 fs mid-IR pulses. Applications now span enzyme catalysis (watching transition states form), membrane protein dynamics, electric fields at protein active sites measured via Stark effect on a CN or carbonyl probe, and the structural dynamics of amyloid intermediates inaccessible to crystallography.

title: Single-Molecule and Ultrafast Spectroscopy
description: smFRET, fs pump-probe, transient absorption, and watching chemistry one molecule at a time

concepts.title: Single-Molecule FRET
concepts.contentHtml:
Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) is dipole–dipole energy transfer from an excited donor fluorophore to a nearby acceptor, with efficiency E = 1/(1 + (r/R0)6). The Förster radius R0 (typically 4–6 nm for common dye pairs like Cy3/Cy5, Atto550/Atto647N, Alexa 488/Alexa 594) makes FRET a 2–10 nm spectroscopic ruler.

Single-molecule FRET (smFRET) watches one molecule at a time, eliminating ensemble averaging that hides intermediate states and asynchronous processes. Two configurations: confocal smFRET with diffusing molecules through a fL excitation volume on a Picoquant MicroTime 200 reveals submillisecond conformational fluctuations; TIRF smFRET on surface-tethered molecules tracks individual trajectories for seconds to minutes.

smFRET has revealed conformational switching of ribosome translation, ribozyme folding intermediates, kinetics of protein folding pathways, voltage-driven motions of membrane proteins, and the mechanism of bacterial RNA polymerase translocation. Pulse-Interleaved Excitation (PIE) and ALEX (alternating laser excitation) cleanly separate FRET-induced from direct-excitation acceptor signal, enabling accurate distance and stoichiometry measurements.

concepts.title: Femtosecond Pump-Probe and Transient Absorption
concepts.contentHtml:
Pump-probe spectroscopy uses an intense femtosecond pump pulse to electronically excite molecules and a delayed weaker probe pulse to read out the resulting absorption changes ΔA(λ, t). Time resolution is set by the pulse cross-correlation, routinely 30–100 fs with Ti:sapphire amplifier systems (Coherent Astrella, Spectra-Physics Solstice Ace) and white-light continuum probes. Helios Fire (Ultrafast Systems) and Newport TA spectrometers turn this into a turnkey lab tool.

The signal contains ground-state bleach (negative ΔA at the absorption peak), stimulated emission (negative, red-shifted), and excited-state absorption (positive). Global fitting with kinetic models (Glotaran, KIMOPACK) extracts species-associated spectra and rate constants for internal conversion, intersystem crossing, charge-transfer, and photoisomerization.

Landmarks: the cis–trans isomerization of rhodopsin in vision occurs in 200 fs; the primary charge separation in photosystem II reaction centers takes ~3 ps; singlet fission in pentacene is complete in ~80 fs. Modern 2D electronic spectroscopy (2DES) applied to FMO and LH2 photosynthetic complexes revealed coherent excitonic dynamics that reignited the entire field of quantum biology.

concepts.title: X-ray Free Electron Lasers and Attosecond Frontiers
concepts.contentHtml:
X-ray Free Electron Lasers (XFELs) — LCLS at SLAC, European XFEL, SACLA, PAL-XFEL, SwissFEL — produce 1012 coherent hard X-ray photons in pulses as short as 1 fs, ten orders of magnitude brighter than synchrotrons. Pump-probe at an XFEL combines time-resolved structure and spectroscopy: serial femtosecond crystallography films enzymes turning over (PSII oxygen evolution, isomerization in rhodopsin), and time-resolved XAS tracks electron and atom motion through transition states with sub-ps temporal and Å spatial resolution.

At the absolute frontier, attosecond spectroscopy (Krausz, L'Huillier, Agostini Nobel 2023) uses high-harmonic-generated XUV pulses of 20–500 attoseconds (1 as = 10−18 s) to time-resolve electron motion within atoms and molecules. Streaking, RABBITT, and attosecond transient absorption record valence electron dynamics, charge migration after photoionization, and the time delay (~20 as) between photoemission of differently bound electrons in Ne — measurements that stretch what 'spectroscopy' can mean.

The arrow has run from minutes (early NMR) to attoseconds (HHG). Each shorter timescale opened a new physics: vibrations on ps, electronic relaxation on fs, electron rearrangement on as. The next spectroscopy is yours to invent.
